abstract.para: Snapshots occupy no additional space when you create them. Their space usage grows as the data of the original subvolume or of the snapshot changes.

section.title: How do snapshots consume space?
section.para: When the system creates a snapshot, the snapshot and the original point to the same blocks in the file system. Initially, a snapshot therefore occupies almost no additional disk space, apart from its metadata.

If data in the original file system is modified, Btrfs copies the changed blocks and keeps the old blocks for the snapshot. Therefore, a snapshot occupies the same amount of space as the data modified. Over time, the space that a snapshot allocates grows constantly.
As a consequence, deleting files from a Btrfs file system that contains snapshots might not free disk space. Btrfs releases a block only when no snapshot and no subvolume references it anymore.

section.title: Checking space usage
section.para: On a Btrfs file system, the output of df can be misleading. In addition to the space for raw data, a Btrfs file system allocates and uses space for metadata. A Btrfs file system can report being out of space although plenty of space seems to be available. In that case, all space allocated for metadata is used up.
Use the following commands to check the space of a Btrfs file system:

variablelist.title: Commands for checking Btrfs space usage

listitem.para: Shows the total size of the file system and its usage. If the two values in the last line match, all space on the file system is allocated.

section.screen: &prompt.sudo;btrfs filesystem du --summarize /mnt/projects-snapshot Total Exclusive Set shared Filename [...]
section.para: The Exclusive value is the amount of space that Btrfs frees when you delete the snapshot.

section.title: Freeing space
section.para: To free space on a Btrfs file system that contains snapshots, delete snapshots that you no longer need. Delete the oldest snapshots first. The older a snapshot is, the more disk space it occupies.
Btrfs reclaims the space of deleted snapshots in a background process. As a result, the free space can become visible with a delay.
If all space is allocated but data chunks are nearly empty, relocate the data with a balance operation. The following command balances data block groups with a usage of 5% or less:

The operation can take many hours on large file systems. The system stays usable during this time. On SUSE Linux Enterprise Server, the timer btrfs-balance.timer cleans up unused block groups every month. You can configure the behavior in the file /etc/sysconfig/btrfsmaintenance.

section.title: Limiting the space of subvolumes
section.para: Subvolumes can use all available disk space during normal operation, which can cause a system malfunction. To prevent this, limit the size of a subvolume with quota groups.

section.para: To remove a limit, set its size to none. To disable quota support for the file system and all subvolumes, run btrfs quota disable. Quota groups add accounting work. On file systems with many snapshots, they can affect performance.

section.title: Planning disk space
section.para: Snapshots always reside on the same partition or subvolume where the snapshot was taken. As a result, partitions that contain snapshots must be larger than partitions without snapshots. The exact amount depends strongly on the number of snapshots that you keep and the amount of data modifications.
As a guideline, plan for twice as much space as you normally would. Automatic tools, such as Snapper, remove old snapshots according to rules.

Before you upgrade a system with a Btrfs root file system, check the free space. In the worst case, the upgrade needs as much disk space as the current root file system for a new snapshot. We recommend having twice as much free space as the current installation uses. The space of old packages becomes free only after Btrfs installs the new packages.
